Symphony control panel

Sign in to take the controls

One press: GitHub asks, the first time only, whether SymphonyBoard may act as you, and sends you straight back here signed in. The token GitHub issues is kept only in this browser, lasts eight hours at a time (the page renews it as you go), and reaches only the repositories SymphonyBoard is installed on, within the App’s permissions and your own access; a small stateless service turns GitHub’s one-time code into that token and keeps nothing.

Sign in with GitHub switches on once its sign-in service is running; until then, use a token below.

Use a fine-grained token instead Make one at github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new: name it, pick the repositories Symphony runs in under Repository access, and under Repository permissions set Actions to Read and write (read lists the runs, write starts a workflow), Checks to Read-only, Contents to Read and write (the read shows the board and the Claude accounts’ readings, the write merges a pull request), Issues to Read and write and Pull requests to Read and write; Metadata comes with them. Adding a Claude account also needs the organization permissions Secrets and Variables set to Read and write. Tracking a drive on the Folders tab also needs the repository permission Secrets set to Read and write. Press Generate token and paste it here. The token is used for GitHub’s API from this browser only; nothing of this site ever receives it. For an organization’s repositories the organization must allow fine-grained tokens (its Settings, Third-party access, Personal access tokens). This is a GitHub token; Claude tokens are made under the Tokens tab’s + Add Token, and the page never sees one.

Board

What this is

The file STATE.md on the branch board, as the board workflow last wrote it: the claims, the open pull requests, the overlaps, the queue, the issues given to workers and the blockers, and, once the repository’s protocol draws them, the dependency charts, which this tab draws in place, each node coloured and edged by its state as the Dependencies tab’s key shows. Rewrite the board from the Command tab to have it read again.

Tasks

How tasks work

The open issues by the protocol’s labels. An issue labelled todo and held by nobody is free for any session or worker to claim; one a worker’s label names waits for that worker; a claim is a branch claude/N. + Add task queues one for the workers, or hands it to @claude at once. Press a card for where it stands, its gear to give it to a worker or ask Claude on it, its × to close it. The Queue, Given and Blocked lists show their tasks in the order the protocol takes them: p1 first, then p2, then p3, then the rest, the oldest first among equals. A card’s ▲ and ▼ raise or lower it one step through those labels, made in the repository the first time one is needed; the workers follow them once the repository runs a release of the protocol that carries them, and until then still take the oldest first. Open the Task form on GitHub for the same with GitHub’s own page.

What the charts show and read

Each open epic’s tasks and what blocks them, drawn as a chart, with the goals above their epics: the chart the board writes into STATE.md once the repository’s protocol can draw it, which the Board tab draws in place. A task is a sub-issue of its epic on GitHub and what blocks it is GitHub’s blocked-by relation, both set on the issue’s page; a goal is an issue labelled goal whose sub-issues are epics. An arrow runs from the issue that blocks to the one it blocks, dotted once the blocker is closed, and a thick one from a goal to its epic; a node’s colour and edge are its state, as the key shows, so no two states differ by colour alone.

Nothing here scrolls: every chart opens whole, and you zoom in where you want to read, with a pinch, the mouse’s wheel, − and + or their keys, or two taps or clicks on a spot; once zoomed in, drag it, and Whole chart or the 0 key draws it whole again. The tiles choose a chart, or All for every chart at once, a page at a time where they are many; Previous and Next, the arrow keys or a swipe across a whole chart step to the one beside it. List shows the same in words in the chart’s place, zoomed the same way.

Press a node to see it in focus: drawn large with only the issues one arrow away, and beside it its state, its worker, its whole title, a link to it on GitHub and Centre its row, which opens the Tasks tab at its row. Press a neighbour, or its number on the card, press an arrow key or swipe the picture as you would a map to move to the neighbour that way; Escape, Whole chart or a pinch outward goes back to the whole chart.

To draw it the page reads, as you, whenever it reads the issues, the sub-issues of each open issue labelled epic or goal and the issues blocking an epic’s tasks: at most sixty reads a draw, none once GitHub says the token has fewer than a hundred calls left this hour, and it writes nothing. The chart is drawn in this browser by a copy of Mermaid the site carries, loaded only when there is a chart to draw.

Explore

How the graph works

The SchwingNet textbook as its search sees it: each chapter is a circle, sized by its sections, the passages Ask the book searches. A solid line joins two chapters where one cites the other; a dashed line joins each chapter to the two whose words are most alike, and the words they share show when you point at it. A title shows when you point at its circle, press it or a search lights it. Press a chapter to list its sections, each a link to its line on GitHub, and the chapters it cites, is cited by and is most like.

Search ranks the sections for your words as the book’s own search does (Okapi BM25, k1 1.5, b 0.75, the same stop words) and lights the chapters that hold the best eight, brightest first, with each passage’s opening words beside the graph.

The book is confidential until the provisional is filed, so nothing of it is in this page: it is read from the private repository OpenSpineConsortium/SchwingNet, through GitHub’s API as you, only when you open this view, and only if your account may read that repository. It is kept in this page’s memory alone and forgotten on a reload or a change of account; nothing is stored or sent anywhere else.

How it works

One epic at a time: its tasks as cards, with the issues outside it that block one of them, and a line from each task to the tasks it blocks, as GitHub holds them (sub-issues and “blocked by”). Ask Claude for ideas opens the Claude box with a question about the epic; the answer’s ideas are drawn here dashed, a new task with Accept, Edit and Dismiss, a new link with Accept and Dismiss. + Task adds a task of your own, and Connect joins two cards: press the task that must be done first, then the task it blocks; a pair already joined on GitHub is added to the changes as a link to remove, and the same pair again takes a waiting change back. A task still Claude’s idea is accepted before it is connected.

What you accept waits under Changes to push, and nothing reaches GitHub until you press Push. The push writes, as you: each new task as an issue labelled todo and made a sub-issue of the epic, then each link as a native “blocked by”. A link that would close a loop is refused, since a task that waits on itself is never free. Undo the last push removes the links it made and closes the issues it opened, as not planned. Claude writes nothing: its ideas come from the assistant issue’s answer, and only your presses act.

    Pull requests

    When Merge can be pressed

    The open pull requests with the state of the checks on each head. Merge becomes pressable once a pull request is ready and every check has passed; it asks once more, then merges with a merge commit, which needs Contents set to Read and write on the token, and the merge closes the issue the pull request says it closes.

    Checks and runs

    What each one starts

    The latest GitHub Actions runs: the required check, the board, the workers, the coordinator, the metrics. Start one by hand: the workers take the queue now instead of at the next six-hourly run, the board is rewritten, the checks run on the default branch, the metrics branch is written.

    Workers

    Where workers are kept

    The registry under .github/symphony/workers/: each routine or worker in Actions is one file there, and a person’s sessions need none. + Add worker opens the “Add a worker” issue; its workflow checks the answers and opens the pull request that adds the file, which joins the registry when it merges. A card’s gear opens a pull request that changes its file, and its × one that removes it; neither changes anything until it merges. Running now lists every worker at work, the grid’s Slurm jobs and the cloud’s runs of the workers workflow, with the issues each holds, its output and the way to stop it. The same form on GitHub: Add a worker.

    Agents

    What an agent is

    An agent is a set of instructions and the tools it may use, kept as a Claude Code subagent file under .claude/agents/ and listed in .github/symphony/agents.json with its purpose. Any session in the repository can hand it work by name; its gear runs it in GitHub Actions on a pull request or issue and sets the tokens it runs on, which is how usage is divided between review, development and testing; and coordbench and flowbench measure the same file. + Import agent brings one in from another repository or an address by pull request, so it joins only once someone merges it; its × opens the pull request that removes it.

    Tokens

    Grid

    How this works

    The Claude accounts signed in on the grid for your Beethoven worker, one in use at a time. The tab is the same whatever repository the panel has open: each press runs the workflow Grid accounts in OpenSpineConsortium/symphony-template, where the grid’s gate is set up, which only an admin may start, and says one word to the grid’s ssh gate; the answer comes back in a few seconds to half a minute. Use moves your running worker to another account at once: its session then shows in that account on claude.ai. Auto mode moves it when its account reaches 90% of a window. Read usage asks each account for one word on Haiku, which spends that word. A sign-in link is sealed for this page alone and opened here with a key that is never stored; e-mails are shown masked.

    Console, at the foot of the tab, shows what a grid job printed, its stdout and stderr: Sign-in output beside an account, Output beside a worker, and the usage job. The grid hides anything shaped like a token before the output leaves it, and the workflow hides it again.

    W&B

    Open in W&B
    How this works

    Your Weights and Biases runs, drawn here from W&B’s own API as you: the projects of your W&B account and its teams, the newest thirty runs of the one chosen, each with its state, when it was last heard from and the last numbers it logged, and, for the run you press, a chart of each metric it logs over its steps, up to four at a time, chosen by the chips over the charts. A running run is read again every fifteen seconds while this tab is shown, and the rest every minute. Open in W&B, and Open this run in W&B beside a run, go to wandb.ai for everything else: media, tables, artifacts, reports and comparisons.

    The key: W&B reads with your API key, which wandb.ai/authorize shows once you are signed in to W&B. Paste it once; the page keeps it in this browser’s storage under the GitHub account you are signed in as, as it keeps a drive’s connection, until Forget W&B or Forget the token, and never writes it into a repository or the address. The key can do on W&B whatever you can, so keep it as you keep a password; this page only reads with it. Each read goes through Symphony’s sign-in service, which passes the query on to W&B with the key and keeps neither, and refuses anything that would change a run, so nothing pressed here changes or deletes one. A key is withdrawn at W&B under API keys at wandb.ai/settings. The grid’s SchwingNet runs log to the project SchwingNet, which is chosen first where your account has it.

    Folders

    How it works

    A repository that tracks files and folders of your OneDrive, one press per step, in Track in a repository. From Track on, the repository’s own workflow, drive-sync.yml, brings what changed in the drive down as a pull request every half hour and sends what changed in the repository back up, and a new comment in a document becomes a task on the board. On a private repository each of those half-hourly runs spends at least a minute of the account’s Actions minutes, about 1,440 a month of GitHub Free’s 2,000 (3,000 on Pro and Team), from the day the repository is made, whether or not it tracks a drive; a public repository spends none. Google Drive comes later, once there is a way that needs no key: Google’s own picker takes a browser API key, which the owner has declined.

    Globus: the second drive, for files on a computing cluster such as Wayne State’s grid, whose Globus collection (wsugrid#globus) this page knows by name. Press + Add a cloud drive, then Connect Globus: Globus asks you to sign in on its own page, with your Globus or university account, and sends you straight back; a collection may ask once more, on the same kind of page, for its own consent. The collection is then drawn here as OneDrive is, read through Globus’s Transfer API as you, starting at your home folder; Up, the tree and a path typed into the search box (starting with /) go anywhere you may read, and Enter looks through the folder shown by name. Double-click a file to open it in a new tab, straight from the collection’s own HTTPS address, where the grid’s Globus server streams it to your browser with no download and no VPN; the first time, Globus asks you to sign in in that tab, and after that files open at once. The preview pane plays a video or a sound from the same address, and fetches an image, a PDF or a text into the page. Download sends the file as a download from the same server. Nothing is written to the collection from here, and nothing of it is tracked: the command bar’s writing verbs and the ticks are OneDrive’s. The connection is kept on this browser as OneDrive’s is, under Forget Globus, and withdrawn at app.globus.org/settings/consents. With both drives connected, each is a root in the folder tree, and a press on the other switches to it. When the collection will not read here, the list says why and links the fix: the same folder in Globus’s own file manager, Connect Globus again, your Globus consents and Globus’s status. Globus moves and streams files only: a shell, a job or Claude Code on the grid is Beethoven’s (what it does, install it in Chrome with an approved account, then press its button in the toolbar). A- and A+ in the head scale this tab’s text with the rest of the console.

    Connect: press + Add a cloud drive, then OneDrive (Google Drive and Dropbox come later). Microsoft asks, on its own page, whether Symphony may read and write your files and keep that access when you are away, and sends you straight back to this tab. A personal OneDrive connects at once; a work or school account may need its organization’s IT department to approve Symphony first, and Microsoft says so on its page. The page then keeps the drive’s refresh token in this browser’s storage for the GitHub account you are signed in as, so a reload, a sign-in that ran out or signing in again as the same account finds OneDrive still connected, and Track in any repository needs no second Connect; another GitHub account on this browser finds none. Forget OneDrive, beside the connection’s name, forgets it on this browser, and Forget the token forgets every connection kept on this browser; Microsoft refusing it, or its 90 days, ends it too. Leaving the page for Microsoft also ends the renewals of a sign-in with GitHub made for this tab alone, whose token still serves for the rest of its eight hours.

    The list: your OneDrive, drawn here from Microsoft Graph as you, in this browser, as Windows’ File Explorer draws a folder: it fills the tab, with the folder tree on the left, Back, Forward, Up and Refresh beside the address, a command bar, the folder’s items in Large icons, Small icons, List, Details, Tiles or Content, sorted by a column’s heading, an optional preview pane (Alt+P), and a search box that narrows the folder shown as you type and searches all of OneDrive when you press Enter. Click, Ctrl+click and Shift+click select as Explorer does. Double-click a Word, Excel or PowerPoint file to open it in that program on your computer, where your edits save straight to the drive (your browser may ask first); any other file opens on OneDrive’s own page, and a right click offers both and Tick. The page reads the drive only once you connect it, as yourself, through Microsoft’s own sign-in. The command bar and a right click work on the drive itself, as you and only when you press them: New folder (Ctrl+Shift+N), Upload (or drop files on the list or on a folder), Cut, Copy and Paste (Ctrl+X, C and V, or drag items onto a folder), Rename (F2), Share, which makes a link only once you press Create link, Delete, which moves what is selected to OneDrive’s recycle bin after you confirm, Download and Properties (Alt+Enter). Tick in the list what to track, then press Track in a repository: Track uses the repository chosen in the bar, and a new one is made only if you open Need a new repository? there. A ticked folder is tracked with everything in it, six levels down. Nothing of the list leaves this browser but the names and ids of what you tick, which go into the repository’s file.

    The repository: GitHub’s own form makes it from the template, named by you, so its first commit stays yours and no App needs to administer it. While the template is internal to OpenSpineConsortium’s enterprise, that form works only for the enterprise’s members; anyone else makes the repository through the front door: install SymphonyBoard and press Create on the form its install leads to, which brings a new or empty repository the whole template, drive-sync.yml with it, by a pull request to merge. The form opens in a new tab; name the repository, press “Create repository”, come back here and press “Find the repository I just made”, which lists it in the bar’s Repository and chooses it. Signed in with GitHub, the page reaches it once SymphonyBoard is installed on it (an installation on all your repositories covers it); a fine-grained token reaches what it was made for, and Track needs it to hold Contents, Secrets and Actions, each Read and write.

    Track writes, as you: the drive’s refresh token, sealed in this browser with GitHub’s public key the way GitHub’s own secrets page seals one, as the secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH, in the repository, or, for a private repository of an organization on a paid plan whose secret no other drive holds, as the organization’s secret, which every private and internal repository of the organization reads, so one Track covers the whole organization, with the variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE_ID beside it naming the drive; the file .github/symphony/drive.json naming the drive, the folder and what you ticked; the repository variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE, set to on, which the half-hourly sync waits for; and the first run of the sync. A repository that only walks the drive, with drive-catalog.yml and no sync, gets the secret alone. On a personal account, which has no secret all its repositories read, Track also renews the secret in each of your other repositories that holds one and tracks the same drive by its file, where that file is dated earlier than the connection; their files keep their date, so their tabs may ask for Connect again sooner than needed. Track dates the file by the day the connection was made, not the day of the press. OneDrive stays connected on this browser after Track. Opening the tab on a repository that already tracks a drive, with its secret set and its connection not known to have run out, sets SYMPHONY_DRIVE to on too, as you, where it was never set, and says so; one set to off is left off. In a public repository the files you tick, their names and the comments in them become readable by anyone, so the tab asks you to confirm before it tracks into one. Where the default branch takes only pull requests, the file waits on a pull request; until it merges, the half-hourly sync runs with the new secret on the file the default branch already holds. Whoever can run a workflow on the repository, anyone who may write to it, can read that secret and, through the sign-in service, reach every file of your OneDrive with it, not only what you ticked, until it lapses or you withdraw Symphony’s access at Microsoft: at account.live.com/consent/Manage for a personal account, or in My Apps for a work or school account, where its administrator may have to. Deleting the secret withdraws nothing at Microsoft. A Microsoft refresh token lasts 90 days, and the run cannot keep the newer one Microsoft issues on each sync, so the tab says when to press Connect OneDrive again, then Track, which replaces the secret and the date; what the repository tracks is ticked already.

    Share

    How access works

    The people GitHub lets into this repository by name, and the invitations still waiting for an answer. + Add people invites someone by GitHub username, or by an email address their GitHub account shows publicly, then opens your own mail with a note that links the invitation. A card’s gear changes its role, and its × takes the access away or withdraws the invitation. Someone who may not push here can press + Ask to join; their request shows at the top for you to Invite, or to decline with its ×. Inviting and changing roles need you to administer the repository and SymphonyBoard’s Administration permission accepted on its installation; without them, GitHub’s own page does the same: Collaborators and teams.

    Notebooks

    What a notebook is and where these come from

    A notebook groups a few of your OneDrive’s files as one context, as NotebookLM does: the files stay where they are, a file may sit in several notebooks, and each notebook is a private repository of its own in which Claude works in the background, keeping its research, its drafts and its references beside what it reads and writing its edits to a file back as tracked changes you accept or reject in Word. Nothing a notebook does can move or lose a file.

    The cards come from the proposal the drive organizer writes, notebooks.json beside catalog.json on the chosen repository’s branch drive-catalog, read here as you; a public repository holds none, and neither does an internal one, which every member of its enterprise can read, since a notebook names a person’s files. Each card shows the notebook’s title, its repository, how many files it holds and their size, their kinds, most common first, and when the newest of them last changed, and says whether its repository is made yet, and whether it is public or internal. Click a card for the notebook’s summary and its files, each with its kind, its last change and a link to it on OneDrive; where its repository is public or internal and you administer it, Make private there makes it private on GitHub as you, after a confirmation that says what GitHub erases with the change (its stars and watchers) and what becomes of its forks.

    + proposes a new notebook: a title, a summary, the name of its repository and the files ticked from the catalog; a card’s gear changes one, and its × takes one out of the proposal, leaving the files on the drive. Each of those writes notebooks.json on the branch drive-catalog as you, with the files no notebook holds listed as left out and whatever else the organizer wrote kept, over the version the cards were drawn from, so a change the organizer made since is never written over: the tab reads the file again and you press again. Taking out the last notebook deletes the file, and whatever else the organizer wrote in it goes too. The repository itself is made from the proposal by the notebook skill in a Claude session, as the template’s tools/notebook.py lays it out; the card says “not found” until it exists or while this sign-in cannot reach it, and warns when it is public or internal.

    About the control panel

    Your Symphony repositories from one console: the board, the queue, the workers, the checks and the pull requests, the Claude accounts, each epic’s tasks and what blocks them drawn as a chart, and a box to ask Claude. The page talks to GitHub’s API as you, from this browser, and, only when you sign in with GitHub or open the Folders tab, to the sign-in service, and, for a drive you connect there, to Microsoft, while your browser fetches the site’s typefaces from Google Fonts as it loads the page; the token stays in this browser. Every state here is written in words and every action is a button or a link with a name, so you and a browsing Claude read and drive it alike. Each tab has its own address: #command, #board, #tasks, #dependencies, #pulls, #runs, #workers, #agents, #tokens, #leaders, #share, #folders, #explore, #notebooks and #about. What it costs, against the other ways of running agents, is on the cost page.

    What this page keeps and sends

    In this browser: the GitHub token, until you press Forget the token. With Keep me signed in ticked, it is kept for every tab of this browser, beside the refresh token GitHub issued with it after Sign in with GitHub, with which the page renews the token after its eight hours. Unticked, the token is kept in this tab’s own storage, which the browser clears when the tab closes and brings back when it reopens or restores the tab, and the refresh token is held by the open page alone, never stored, so the renewals end once that page is gone (closed, reloaded, or replaced by another page such as the cost page) and that sign-in ends with its eight-hour token. Also kept: the names of the repositories you listed, the layout you set (the sizes you dragged the parts to, the text size, whether the tabs open as buttons or as the legacy side rail, and the order you dragged the buttons to), the plan you chose on the cost page, the number of the assistant issue the page uses in each repository, one it opened or found, and which chart you last chose on each repository’s Dependencies tab, by the repository’s name and the chart’s, until you choose another, which neither Forget the token nor taking the repository off your list removes. In this tab’s own storage, from a press of Sign in with GitHub until GitHub’s return reaches the page: a one-time value, the sign-in’s one-time secret, whether Keep me signed in is ticked and the page’s query (the repository it showed); for a sign-in that never comes back it stays, and Forget the token does not clear it, until another press of Sign in with GitHub replaces it, a return from GitHub or from Microsoft reaches the tab, or the browser clears the tab’s own storage. Sent: each time the page loads, unless your browser holds them from an earlier load, a request from your browser to Google Fonts for the site’s typefaces (Newsreader, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono) and, as the text needs them, for the font files they name, as on the site’s other Symphony pages, requests that name the site by its address or origin alone and carry nothing of the page’s own, no token, no repository’s name and nothing you type, though Google sees your network address and the headers your browser sends with every request, under its own privacy policy, and the developer receives nothing of them; requests to GitHub’s API, as you, for what the page shows and does (a question to the assistant goes as a comment on that issue, and the page reads the issue’s comments every few seconds while it waits for the answer; for the Dependencies tab the page reads the sub-issues of each open epic or goal and the issues blocking each of an epic’s sub-issues, draws them in this browser with a copy of Mermaid loaded from this site only when there is a chart to draw, as it draws the board’s own charts in the Board tab, and stores nothing of them but which chart you chose: the chart is gone with the page), and nothing to anyone else, a token you paste included, which GitHub is asked about before the page keeps it, beyond the requests to Google Fonts above; on the Folders tab, what it sends for a drive (below); on the Notebooks tab, reads of notebooks.json and catalog.json on the repository’s branch drive-catalog and of whether each notebook’s repository exists and is private, and, when you propose, change or take out a notebook, a write of notebooks.json there, all sent to GitHub as you; on the Share tab, reads of who has access and which invitations wait, an invitation to the GitHub user you name and, when you press a person’s gear or ×, a new role, a removal or a withdrawn invitation, all sent to GitHub as you, and an address you type to GitHub’s user search to find that user, while its mail buttons open Gmail, Outlook, your email app or your device’s share sheet with a note you send yourself; with Sign in with GitHub, GitHub’s one-time code to the sign-in service, which answers with the token and keeps nothing, the refresh token to the same service when the token is renewed, and a sign-in’s token once more when you press Forget the token, or sign in or paste a token GitHub accepts over it, so that GitHub revokes it; and signing in by code (in the Home Screen app, or with Sign in with a code instead), a request to the same service for a code, which it asks GitHub for with SymphonyBoard’s client id alone, then the device code GitHub gave with it, held in the open page’s memory alone and sent to the same service every five seconds, or more slowly when GitHub asks, until you have typed the short code on GitHub’s page and GitHub answers with the token, GitHub refuses, the code runs out, or you press Cancel, sign in another way or forget the token, and a token GitHub gives for a code the page has let go of once more, so that GitHub revokes it; Copy it and open GitHub puts the short code on your device’s clipboard, for you to paste on GitHub’s page. The developer receives nothing from this page. The Apps’ privacy statement, which covers it, is at /symphony/apps-privacy.html.

    On the Folders tab, in this tab’s own storage while the browser is at Microsoft, and forgotten on its return: a one-time value, a one-time secret, the panel’s query (the repository it showed) and the GitHub login the panel names. In this browser’s storage, by GitHub account, until Forget OneDrive, Forget the token, Microsoft refusing it or 90 days after it was issued: the drive’s refresh token, the day it was issued, and the drive’s type, owner’s name and id. In the open page’s memory alone, until a reload or leaving the page, Forget OneDrive, Forget the token or any other sign-out, or a sign-in as another GitHub account: the drive’s access token, and, until a reload or leaving the page, the explorer’s view, sort order, preview switch, what you chose, what you cut or copied, the words you searched for and the preview’s addresses. Sent: when the tab first opens, a question to the sign-in service about which drives it is set up for, answered with a public client id; Microsoft’s one-time code to the sign-in service, which adds the client secret it holds, answers with the two tokens and keeps nothing; the refresh token to the same service when the access token runs out during a sitting; requests to Microsoft Graph, as you, for the drive’s type, its owner’s name and its id and for the list you browse, with a small picture of each file, which your browser loads from Microsoft with no token and no referrer; to Microsoft Graph, as you, only when you press it: a new folder, a new name, a deletion into the recycle bin, the files you upload (a large one in pieces to the address Microsoft gives, with no token), a request for a file’s download address (your browser then saves the file from Microsoft with no token), a move or a copy, a sharing link for viewing or editing made only on Create link, one item’s properties, a file’s preview or larger picture, and, on Enter, the words you search the whole drive for; and to GitHub’s API, as you, a read of the names at the top of the default branch, so that no folder the repository already holds there is tracked into, then the sealed secret, on a personal account the list of your repositories with, for each, whether it holds the secret and what its file tracks, and the sealed secret again in each that tracks the same drive, the file (on the default branch or, where that takes only pull requests, on the branch symphony/drive with a pull request) and the request to run the sync. The repository’s own run then trades the secret for an access token at the same service on every sync; whoever can run a workflow on the repository can do the same with it, until it lapses or you withdraw Symphony’s access at Microsoft. The developer receives nothing from this tab either.
